final_proof:
Let an object of the comma category \((\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}\downarrow F)\) be written \((E,*,g)\). By definition, its structure arrow is
\[
g:\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}(E)=E\longrightarrow F(*)=C.
\]
Thus \(g:E\to C\) is an object of the slice category \(\mathbf C/C\), so \(J(E,*,g)=g\) is well-defined.

Now let
\[
(k,\operatorname{id}_*):(E,*,g)\longrightarrow(E',*,g')
\]
be a morphism in the comma category. Its second component is necessarily \(\operatorname{id}_*\), since \(\mathbf 1\) has only one morphism. The comma-category compatibility equation is
\[
F(\operatorname{id}_*)\circ g
   =g'\circ\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}(k).
\]
Because \(F(\operatorname{id}_*)=\operatorname{id}_C\) and the identity functor sends \(k\) to \(k\), this equation becomes
\[
g=g'\circ k.
\]
This is precisely the condition for \(k:E\to E'\) to be a morphism from the slice object \(g:E\to C\) to the slice object \(g':E'\to C\). Hence \(J(k,\operatorname{id}_*)=k\) is well-defined and has the required source and target.

It remains to verify the functor laws. The identity morphism of \((E,*,g)\) in the comma category is \((\operatorname{id}_E,\operatorname{id}_*)\). Therefore
\[
J(\operatorname{id}_E,\operatorname{id}_*)=\operatorname{id}_E,
\]
which is the identity morphism of the slice object \(g:E\to C\).

Suppose
\[
(k,\operatorname{id}_*):(E,*,g)\to(E',*,g')
\quad\text{and}\quad
(\ell,\operatorname{id}_*):(E',*,g')\to(E'',*,g'')
\]
are composable. Composition in a comma category is componentwise, so
\[
(\ell,\operatorname{id}_*)\circ(k,\operatorname{id}_*)
=(\ell\circ k,\operatorname{id}_*\circ\operatorname{id}_*)
=(\ell\circ k,\operatorname{id}_*).
\]
Consequently,
\[
J\bigl((\ell,\operatorname{id}_*)\circ(k,\operatorname{id}_*)\bigr)
=\ell\circ k
=J(\ell,\operatorname{id}_*)\circ J(k,\operatorname{id}_*).
\]
Thus \(J\) preserves identities and composition. Therefore
\[
J:(\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}\downarrow F)\longrightarrow\mathbf C/C
\]
is a covariant functor.
